query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A mild oxidative pre‐treatment that induces the in‐situ formation of a disordered, multi‐component oxide passivation layer on the near‐equiatomic alloy catalyst will simultaneously lower the light‐off temperatures for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation, improve resistance to poisoning (by H2O and NO), and enhance long‐term durability without raising the platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with a largely metallic, unmodified surface.
generation.intervention: Expose the catalyst to a controlled, mild oxidation (thermal pre‐treatment in a dilute O2/air atmosphere) to promote the formation of a thin, high-entropy oxide surface layer that incorporates any trace PGMs already present without additional loading.
generation.conditions: The modified catalyst is used under simulated automotive exhaust conditions that include transient low-temperature operation (below 150 °C during cold start), exposure to typical concentrations of water vapor (~10 vol%), NO and hydrocarbon species, and cyclical high-temperature aging (up to 800–850 °C) to simulate vehicle lifetime stress.
generation.structural_mediator: An in‐situ formed, disordered high-entropy oxide layer that exhibits lattice distortion and abundant oxygen vacancies, which acts as a protective and active interfacial medium.
generation.mechanism: The oxide passivation layer serves multiple functions: (1) its disordered and strained structure improves low-temperature activation by facilitating the formation of reactive oxygen species; (2) it reduces the adsorption strength of poisoning species such as H2O and NO on the active sites; and (3) by hindering atomic diffusion, it retards sintering and preserves catalyst morphology over prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the treated catalyst is predicted to achieve a marked reduction (e.g., on the order of 20–30% lower light-off temperatures) for complete oxidation, exhibit less deactivation (by at least 10% less activity loss over accelerated aging tests), and maintain catalytic activity under poisoning conditions—all without an increase in the amount of platinum-group metals.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (activity, poisoning resistance, and longevity) of the original untreated near‐equiatomic alloy catalyst under the same exhaust and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention will be effective only if the mild oxidation creates a controlled oxide layer without excessive loss of metallic active sites; excessive oxidation that overshadows the active alloy interior or forms overly thick passivation could negate activity improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, thickness, and structural configuration of the oxide layer depend on the pre‐treatment parameters and alloy composition; the optimal oxidation conditions need to be established experimentally while ensuring the trade-off between enhanced stability and preserved activity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst batches: one unmodified and one subjected to the controlled mild oxidation pre‐treatment. Expose both batches to a series of simulated automotive exhaust cycles that include transient low-temperature operation, high water vapor and NO concentrations, and accelerated thermal aging. Compare the catalytic performance (light-off temperatures, conversion rates, and deactivation profiles) and conduct surface characterizations (e.g., XPS, TEM) before and after the tests.
measurements: Light-off temperatures (T50/T100) for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Catalytic conversion rates under dry and humid conditions
Activity retention percentage over long-term accelerated aging
Surface morphology and oxide layer thickness via TEM/XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidatively pre-treated catalyst does not demonstrate at least a 20% reduction in light-off temperatures and achieves less than a 10% improvement in deactivation rate (compared to the untreated catalyst) under identical simulated exhaust conditions, or if excessive oxidation is observed degrading the exposure of active sites, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractEnhancing the activity and stability of earth‐abundant, heterogeneous catalysts remains a key challenge, requiring new materials design strategies to replace platinum‐group metals. Herein, it is demonstrated that increasing the configurational disorder of spinel metal oxides (M3O4, where M is a combination of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) leads to significant improvements in carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation performance. A substantial 63% decrease in the T10 value (temperature to reach 10% CO oxidation) is observed by systematically increasing the number of first‐row transition metals within the spinel oxide. Long‐term stability studies reveal that the most disordered 7‐metal spinel oxide exhibited superior resistance to catalyst deactivation compared to the 4‐metal variant, showing a decrease in activity of only 4.7% versus 12.2% during 14 h of operation. A solventless thermolysis approach is developed to synthesize a series of medium entropy spinel oxide (MESO) and high entropy spinel oxides (HESOs) from discrete, air‐stable molecular precursors. cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation.
